pos: n. (Immanuel Tremellius, 1510–1580, Ferrarese Jew converted to Christ, Hebraist and translator of the Old Testament into Latin)
etymology: Hebrew Immanuel, God with us, taken at baptism; Tremellius, latinised from the Ferrarese family name Tremellio.
biblical_def: Immanuel Tremellius was born a Jew at Ferrara and baptised in 1540 in the household of Cardinal Pole, who stood sponsor; within a year Peter Martyr Vermigli had brought him from Rome to the Reformed faith, and he left Italy with Vermigli in 1542. He taught Hebrew at Strasbourg, followed Vermigli to England, and under Edward VI held the Regius chair of Hebrew at Cambridge; Mary's reign sent him back to the Rhineland, where he taught at Hornbach and Heidelberg and at last, driven out by the Lutheran reaction in the Palatinate, at the new academy of Sedan, where he died. His monument is the Latin Old Testament translated directly from the Hebrew, completed with his son-in-law Franciscus Junius and printed from 1575, which Reformed divines used for two centuries beside the Vulgate and generally in preference to it. A Hebrew Christian who spent forty years giving the church the Hebrew Scriptures in a tongue its ministers could read is the standing answer to the notion that the Reformation had no place for Israel. “Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved” (Rom 10:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Hebraist as one versed in the Hebrew language, and a version as a translation from one language into another.
webster_full: HE'BRAIST, n. One versed in the Hebrew language and literature.
VER'SION, n. A translation; a change of a writing from one language into another.
PROS'ELYTE, n. A new convert to some religion or religious sect.
ORIG'INAL, n. First copy; archetype; that from which anything is translated or copied.
scriptures: Rom 10:1
Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved.
Rom 9:4
Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises;
Rom 11:1
I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: The Ferrarese Jew who gave the Reformed churches their Latin Old Testament.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a double one. Tremellius is cited by some as evidence that the Reformation was indifferent to the Jews, a scholar valued only for his grammar; and he is cited by others as a man who abandoned his people. Neither reading survives the Junius-Tremellius Old Testament, which exists because he thought the Hebrew text and the Hebrew people both mattered more than his own comfort in three countries that successively expelled him.

The principle to recover is that Paul's burden for Israel is not a sentiment the church may drop and not a programme it may substitute for the gospel. He states the privileges without retracting a word of them — “to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law” (Rom 9:4) — and he answers the question of their rejection in his own person: “For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom 11:1).

Greek huiothesia (G5206) — adoption, the placing as a son; Romans 9:4.

“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — the ground of forty years at the Hebrew text.
“Hath God cast away his people? God forbid” (Rom 11:1) — the question his life answered.

pos: n. (Giovanni Diodati, 1576–1649, Genevan divine of Lucchese exile stock, translator of the Italian Bible)
etymology: Italian Giovanni, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Diodati, given of God, from Latin Deodatus.
biblical_def: Giovanni Diodati was born at Geneva to a merchant house that had fled Lucca for the faith. He was made professor of Hebrew at nineteen, succeeded Theodore Beza in the chair of theology in 1609, and served the Genevan church for half a century. In 1607 he published the Italian Bible that bears his name, translated from the Hebrew and Greek and furnished with annotations, revised in 1641 with the metrical psalms; it remains the Bible of Italian Protestantism to this day. He made a French version as well, and the English Parliament had his notes translated in 1643, so that English Puritans read Diodati on their own Bibles. He was one of the delegates to the Synod of Dort and stood with the strictest party there against the Remonstrants. His life answers a question the Italian Reformation otherwise leaves open: what the exiles' children did with their fathers' losses. They printed the Scriptures in the tongue their fathers had been driven out of. “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an annotation as a remark or note on a text, and to expound as to explain or lay open the sense.
webster_full: ANNOTA'TION, n. A remark, note or commentary on some passage of a book, intended to illustrate its meaning.
EXPOUND', v. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
DIS'TINCTLY, adv. Not confusedly; plainly; clearly; with clear and distinct utterance.
SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
scriptures: Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Act 8:30
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: The exiles' son who gave Italy its Protestant Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a modern one about translation itself: that a version carrying doctrinal notes is by that fact a partisan Bible, while a bare text is neutral. Diodati's notes are confessedly Reformed, and he said so on the title page; the pretence of neutrality belongs to versions that smuggle their theology into the rendering instead of printing it in the margin where a reader can weigh it.

The principle to recover is that translation and exposition are two offices and both are owed to the people. Ezra's Levites did not stop at reading — they “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — and Philip's question to the eunuch assumes that a man may have the text and still want the sense: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30).

“Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30) — the question a translator serves.
“from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15) — what an Italian household gained in 1607.

pos: n. (Antonio Bruccioli, c. 1498–1566, Florentine who made the first complete Italian Bible from the original tongues)
etymology: Italian Antonio, from the Roman gens Antonius; Bruccioli, a Florentine family name.
biblical_def: Antonio Bruccioli was a Florentine of republican politics, exiled from the city in 1522 for a plot against the Medici and settled in Venice as a bookseller and translator. Between 1530 and 1532 he published the New Testament and then the whole Bible in Italian, translated from the Hebrew and Greek rather than from the Vulgate — the first complete Italian version made from the originals, and for a generation the Bible of every Italian who wanted one. He followed it with a vast commentary drawn largely from Reformed and humanist sources. Rome put the Bible and the commentary on the Index, tried him in 1548 and again in 1555, made him abjure, and he died in poverty in Venice under house arrest. His case is the plainest proof that the Italian Reformation was strangled rather than refused: a vernacular Bible existed, it was read, and it was suppressed by a tribunal, not abandoned by a people. “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vernacular tongue as the native language of a country, and an index as a list, here of books prohibited.
webster_full: VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
IN'DEX, n. A table of contents; among the Romanists, a catalogue of prohibited books.
TRANSLA'TION, n. The act of turning into another language; a version.
SUPPRESS', v. To crush; to subdue; to keep in; to conceal from the public.
scriptures: Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Amo 8:11
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
corruption_summary: The first Italian Bible from the Hebrew and Greek, and the tribunal that buried it.
corruption_paragraphs: A standing claim in Roman apologetic is that the Church never withheld the Scriptures from the laity and that vernacular Bibles circulated freely before the Reformation; Bruccioli is the awkward case. His version was not a heretic's smuggled text but a printed book openly sold in Venice, and it was the Index and the Holy Office, not the market, that ended it. A church that tries a translator twice and keeps him under arrest until he dies has withheld the Scriptures, whatever its theory allowed.

The principle to recover is that the word of God is not fragile and does not depend on the permission of magistrates for its continuance: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). What a tribunal can do is starve a generation, and Amos names that judgment exactly — “a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11).

“but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — what the Index could not reach.
“a famine in the land, not a famine of bread” (Amo 8:11) — what it could.

pos: n. (Massimo Teofilo, c. 1509–after 1555, Florentine Benedictine who translated the New Testament into Italian)
etymology: Italian Massimo, from Latin Maximus, greatest; Teofilo, from Greek Theophilos, lover of God — a name taken in religion.
biblical_def: Massimo Teofilo was a Florentine who took the Benedictine habit in the Cassinese congregation, the one religious order in Italy where the doctrine of free justification was read and discussed without immediate reprisal. He published at Lyons in 1551 an Italian New Testament translated from the Greek, with prefaces that set out salvation by faith in Christ alone, and he dedicated it to the Duke of Ferrara. He was a reformer who never left the cloister; the Cassinese house gave him shelter long enough to finish the work and not long enough to protect him afterwards, and he disappears from the record after the middle of the century. His version was read where Bruccioli's could no longer be had. He stands for a company larger than the histories show: men inside the Italian religious orders who came to the gospel over an open Greek Testament and put what they found into the language of their countrymen. “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Benedictine as a monk of the order of St Benedict, and to search as to look over carefully in order to find something.
webster_full: BENEDIC'TINE, n. One of the order of monks founded by Benedict, abbot of Mount Cassino.
SEARCH, v. To look over or through for the purpose of finding something; to explore; to examine.
PREF'ACE, n. Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book.
CLOIS'TER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a house inhabited by monks or nuns.
scriptures: Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: The Benedictine who put the Greek New Testament into Italian and never left his cloister.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the romantic one: the evangelical monk is held up as proof that the Reformation was unnecessary, since the gospel could be recovered inside the old structures without a division. Teofilo's own end is the refutation. The order that let him read sheltered no one when the Holy Office moved, and the Cassinese evangelicals left no church behind them.

The principle to recover is the Berean one, which is not a scholar's privilege but a congregation's duty, and which requires a text in a tongue the congregation has: “they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). Luke commends them for checking an apostle. A church that cannot read cannot obey that commendation, which is why the translators matter.

“searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — the duty a translation makes possible.
“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16) — his aim for Italian households.

pos: n. (Lucio Paolo Rosello, d. c. 1556, Paduan priest and political writer tried at Venice for heresy)
etymology: Italian Lucio, from Latin Lucius, of light; Paolo, from Latin Paulus, little; Rosello, a Paduan family name.
biblical_def: Lucio Paolo Rosello was a priest of Padua who lived by his pen in Venice, editing and writing in the busiest print trade in Europe. His Ritratto del vero governo del prencipe of 1552 set out the duties of a Christian ruler from Scripture against the counsels of expediency then fashionable, and other works of his circulated the doctrine of justification by faith under cover of moral and political discourse. He was denounced to the Holy Office, examined, and compelled to abjure in 1551; a second process followed, and he died in prison or shortly after release about 1556. He matters to this dictionary chiefly because of what he attempted: to apply the recovered gospel to the magistrate's office at the moment when Italian presses were producing the opposite counsel, and to insist that a prince is under a law he did not make. “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth” (Psa 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a magistrate as a public civil officer invested with authority, and policy as the art or manner of governing a nation.
webster_full: MAG'ISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government of some branch of it.
POL'ICY, n. The art, prudence or wisdom of government; management of public affairs.
PRINCE, n. A sovereign; the chief and independent ruler of a nation or state.
EXPE'DIENCY, n. Fitness or suitableness to effect some good end; sometimes, mere advantage.
scriptures: Psa 2:10
Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
It is an abomination to kings to commit wickedness: for the throne is established by righteousness.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
corruption_summary: The Venetian pamphleteer who put the prince under the law of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Rosello wrote into a market that Machiavelli had formed, where the ruler's art was taught as the management of appearances and the measure of a policy was whether it held. That teaching did not die with the sixteenth century; it is the working creed of every administration that treats law as an instrument and conscience as a cost. Rosello's answer was neither a counsel of withdrawal nor a scheme for a godly tyranny but the simple assertion that the magistrate is a minister with a master.

The principle to recover is that civil authority is derivative and therefore accountable: “For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1). The same ordination that requires the subject's obedience binds the ruler's hands, and Solomon states the consequence a people feels first: “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2).

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, right, power; Romans 13:1.

“for the throne is established by righteousness” (Pro 16:12) — against the counsel of expediency.
“there is no power but of God” (Rom 13:1) — why a magistrate is accountable.

pos: n. (Francesco Negri, 1500–c. 1564, Benedictine of Bassano who left the cloister for the Grisons and wrote against free will)
etymology: Italian Francesco, the Frenchman, from Late Latin Franciscus; Negri, black, from Latin niger.
biblical_def: Francesco Negri of Bassano entered the Benedictines, read Luther, and in 1525 walked out of the cloister — one of the earliest Italians to do so openly. He went to Strasbourg, married, and settled at Chiavenna in the Grisons, the Protestant valley on the Italian side of the Alps that became the refuge of a whole generation of Italian evangelicals, where he kept a school for thirty years. In 1546 he printed at Venice, under the cover of a play, the Tragedia del libero arbitrio, a dramatised attack on the freedom of the will which went through several editions and was answered across Italy; it is the most widely read Italian statement of the Reformed doctrine of grace. His later years were troubled by the anti-Trinitarian currents of the Grisons, and his son went over to them, which he lived to see and to grieve. The doctrine he staked his book on is Paul's: “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines free will as the power of directing our own actions without constraint, and grace as the free unmerited favour of God.
webster_full: WILL, n. The faculty of the mind by which we determine either to do or forbear an action; choice; determination.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favour of God; the divine influence which renews the heart.
BOND'AGE, n. Slavery or involuntary servitude; captivity; imprisonment; restraint of a person's liberty.
TRAG'EDY, n. A dramatic poem representing some signal action performed by illustrious persons.
scriptures: Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Joh 8:36
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
corruption_summary: The Bassano Benedictine whose stage-play argued the bondage of the will.
corruption_paragraphs: The free will Negri wrote against is not a dead doctrine but the common assumption of modern religion, restated as a defence of human dignity: that a choice which is not finally the man's own cannot be a real choice, and that a God who gives the will its decision has taken something from the man. The objection mistakes the diagnosis. Scripture does not describe a neutral will waiting to be solicited but a dead man, and a corpse is not flattered by being told the decision is his.

The principle to recover is that grace is not assistance offered to the willing but life given to the dead, and liberty is its fruit and not its condition. “And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1) is the state the gospel finds; “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44) is the Lord's own statement of the impossibility; and the freedom that follows is a gift: “If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed” (Joh 8:36).

roots_lines: Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, wish, desire; Romans 9:16.
Greek eleeo (G1653) — to have mercy, show compassion; Romans 9:16.
Greek helko (G1670) — to draw, drag, compel; John 6:44.
Greek suzoopoieo (G4806) — to make alive together with; Ephesians 2:5.
Greek eleutheroo (G1659) — to make free, set at liberty; John 8:36.

“who were dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1) — the condition free will overlooks.
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed” (Joh 8:36) — the only liberty he would grant the will.

pos: n. (Il Beneficio di Cristo, 1543, the most widely read evangelical book of the Italian Reformation)
etymology: Italian, the benefit of Christ: beneficio from Latin beneficium, a kindness, benefit; Cristo from Greek Christos, anointed.
biblical_def: Il Beneficio di Cristo, printed at Venice in 1543 under the full title of a treatise on the most useful benefit of Christ crucified toward Christians, was written by a Benedictine of Mantua, Don Benedetto Fontanini, and polished by the poet Marcantonio Flaminio of the Valdésian circle. It is a short, warm, unargumentative book on the free pardon of the sinner through the imputed righteousness of Christ, drawing on Calvin's Institutes and on Valdes without naming either. It sold on a scale nothing else in Italian religion approached — the contemporary estimate is forty thousand copies in Venice alone in six years — and it was read in convents, at court and in shops. The Holy Office put it on the Index of 1549 and pursued it so thoroughly that for three centuries no Italian copy was known to survive; the book was recovered in the nineteenth century from an English translation and then from a single copy at Cambridge. It is the Italian Reformation's one popular classic. “Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom 5:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a benefit as an act of kindness or a favour conferred, and imputation as the attribution of something to a person.
webster_full: BEN'EFIT, n. An act of kindness; a favour conferred; advantage; profit.
IMPUTA'TION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution; the reckoning of righteousness to a believer.
TREAT'ISE, n. A written composition on a particular subject, in which the principles of it are discussed.
EDI'TION, n. The publication of a book; the whole number of copies published at once.
scriptures: Rom 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
corruption_summary: The little Venetian book on free pardon that the Index nearly erased.
corruption_paragraphs: Because the Beneficio names no party and quotes no Reformer, it is regularly produced as evidence of a third way: an Italian evangelism that was neither Roman nor Protestant and that the confessional age destroyed from both sides. The book itself will not bear the weight. Its doctrine of the sinner's acceptance is the Reformed doctrine, taken in substance from the Institutes, and the Holy Office read it correctly and condemned it for exactly that. Its irenic manner was a tactic of survival, not a theology.

The principle to recover is that the gospel can be stated warmly and briefly without being stated vaguely, and that the gracious note of the Beneficio rests on a hard exchange: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21). Take away the imputation and the comfort has nothing under it; keep it, and a book of forty pages can carry a nation.
roots_lines: Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, justify; Romans 5:1.
Greek eirene (G1515) — peace, concord; Romans 5:1.
Greek hamartia (G266) — sin, a missing of the mark; 2 Corinthians 5:21.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, count, impute; Romans 4:5.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace, unmerited favour; Ephesians 2:8.
usage: “Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Rom 5:1) — the book's whole burden.
“him that justifieth the ungodly” (Rom 4:5) — the phrase the Index could not tolerate.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith” (Eph 2:8) — forty thousand Venetian copies of it.

pos: n. pl. (the Reformed congregation of Locarno, expelled in 1555 and received at Zurich)
etymology: Locarno, a town on Lake Maggiore in the Swiss-governed Ticino; exile from Latin exilium, banishment.
biblical_def: Locarno lay in the Italian-speaking lands south of the Alps governed jointly by the Swiss cantons, so that a Reformed congregation could gather there under Swiss protection while standing on Italian soil. It did gather, from about 1540, and grew into the one organised evangelical church in an Italian town. In 1554 the Catholic cantons carried a vote in the federal diet requiring the Locarnesi to return to the mass or depart, and in March 1555 something over a hundred of them — men, women and children, with the aged and the infants among them — crossed the Alps in the last of the winter to Zurich, where Bullinger received them and the city gave them a church. They became an Italian congregation of Zurich and in time Zurich families: the Muralts, the Orellis, the Pestalozzis descend from them. Their departure ended the Reformation on the Italian peninsula as an organised thing. “These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off” (Heb 11:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exile as banishment from one's country, and a pilgrim as a wanderer, one who travels to a distance from his own country.
webster_full: EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country.
PIL'GRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveller; one that travels to a distance from his own country.
CON'GREGATION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God and for religious instruction.
STRAN'GER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; a guest.
scriptures: These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come.
corruption_summary: The one organised Italian Reformed church, driven over the Alps in the winter of 1555.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a quiet one: the expulsion is told as a Swiss constitutional episode, a question of jurisdiction in the subject lands, with the hundred and more people walking an Alpine pass in March reduced to a consequence of a federal vote.

The principle to recover is that exile is a biblical category and not merely a misfortune, and that the church has always had to sing in places it did not choose: “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4). The answer the Locarnesi gave is the one Hebrews gives, that the settled city was never the thing promised — “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).

pos: n. (the Italian stranger congregation in London, founded 1550, revived 1570)
etymology: Italian from Latin Italia; stranger church, the Tudor term for a congregation of resident foreigners worshipping in its own tongue.
biblical_def: The Italian Church of London was one of the stranger congregations chartered under Edward VI in 1550, when the young king's council gave the exiled Protestants of Europe the former Austin Friars and a liberty to worship in their own languages and under their own discipline. The Italian body was small beside the Dutch and French but it gathered the refugees that Italy was then producing, and its first minister was Michelangelo Florio, a former Franciscan of Tuscany, whose son John Florio became the translator of Montaigne and a figure of the English Renaissance. Mary's accession in 1553 scattered all the stranger churches; the Italians re-formed under Elizabeth about 1570 and worshipped for some generations before dwindling into the larger English and French congregations. The arrangement mattered out of all proportion to its size: a Reformed city gave foreigners a church in their own tongue with its own elders, and a persecuted remnant was treated not as a charity but as a church. “Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints” (Eph 2:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a stranger as a foreigner who belongs to another country, and a tongue as a language or the speech of a nation.
webster_full: STRAN'GER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not a citizen.
TONGUE, n. The whole sum of words used by a particular nation; a language.
FEL'LOWCITIZEN, n. A citizen of the same state or city with another.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. In a church, the exercise of government and correction over members.
scriptures: Eph 2:19
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Act 2:11
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
corruption_summary: A Tudor charter that gave Italian refugees a church in their own tongue.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs the other way: the stranger churches are now cited as an early model of multicultural accommodation, a toleration of difference for its own sake. Edward's council tolerated nothing of the kind. The charter was granted to Reformed congregations holding a Reformed confession and submitting to a Reformed discipline, and it was a recognition of churches, not a celebration of variety.

The principle to recover is that language is a servant of understanding in worship and never an ornament. Paul will trade rhetorical splendour for comprehension without hesitating: “Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue” (1Co 14:19). A congregation of Italians in London therefore needed Italian preaching, and Pentecost had already settled the principle: “And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8).

pos: n. (Juan Díaz, c. 1510–1546, Spanish evangelical murdered at Neuburg by his own brother)
etymology: Spanish Juan, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Díaz, son of Diego, from Didacus.
biblical_def: Juan Díaz was a Spaniard of Cuenca who studied thirteen years in Paris and was reckoned among the best Hebraists there. He came to the Reformed faith, went to Geneva, and then to Strasbourg, where Martin Bucer took him as a colleague and sent him with the Strasbourg delegation to the colloquy at Ratisbon in 1546. There he was approached by Spanish agents and then by his own brother Alfonso, an advocate of the Roman Rota who had ridden from Rome when he heard the news. Alfonso argued, offered money, failed, and left; then he turned back, and on the morning of 27 March 1546 sent his servant into the house at Neuburg where Juan was lodging, who split his skull with a hatchet. The brothers were arrested and were released by the emperor's court; no punishment followed. The crime shocked Protestant Germany and was printed everywhere, and Bucer wrote the account. “Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother” (1Jo 3:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fratricide as the murder of a brother, and a colloquy as a conference or mutual discourse of two or more.
webster_full: FRAT'RICIDE, n. The crime of murdering a brother; also, one who murders a brother.
COL'LOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a conference.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardour in the pursuit of anything; in religion, ardour in the pursuit of what one believes.
AV'ENGE, v. To take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injuring party.
scriptures: Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous.
Gen 4:8
And Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.
And the brother shall deliver up the brother to death, and the father the child: and the children shall rise up against their parents, and cause them to be put to death.
Rev 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
corruption_summary: The Spanish Hebraist killed at his brother's order, and acquitted murderers.
corruption_paragraphs: The Díaz murder is sometimes offered as an instance of sixteenth-century fanaticism in general, as though the two brothers were equally carried away by the passions of a confessional age and the lesson were the folly of taking doctrine seriously. The symmetry is false. One brother held a conviction and was struck down for it; the other hired a hatchet and was let go by a court. The age's sin was not that men believed things but that a tribunal would not punish a murder committed on the right side.

The principle to recover is that the Lord foretold precisely this division and did not soften it: “And the brother shall deliver up the brother to death” (Mat 10:21). John names the first case and the motive together — “And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous” (1Jo 3:12) — and the martyrs under the altar are permitted to ask for the justice that Neuburg did not get: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood” (Rev 6:10).
